title: Why Behavior Contracts Don't Work
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the common practice of using individualized behavior contracts for difficult students, arguing that despite their popularity and initial effectiveness, they cause more harm than good. He contends that treating a student differently from peers communicates that the student is fundamentally different and unable to control himself, a label that becomes self-fulfilling. He also argues that the external rewards typical of behavior contracts lose their motivational power quickly, and that contracts which depend on parent follow-through are unreliable because parental support fades. His alternative is to apply the same classroom management plan, rules, and consequences to every student without exception, arguing that a well-run plan does not label students the way a contract does. The article positions the classroom management plan as the more durable, less stigmatizing tool for improving behavior.
points: Treating a difficult student differently through an individualized contract can label them as fundamentally 'other,' which becomes self-fulfilling.
External rewards used in most behavior contracts motivate only in the short term before their novelty wears off.
Contracts that depend on consistent parental follow-through are unreliable because parental engagement fades over time.
Applying one classroom management plan equally to every student avoids stigmatizing labels while still holding students accountable.
quotes: Anytime you treat difficult students differently than everyone else—by applying a different set of rules, incentives, and consequences—you’re communicating to them that they’re different, that they can’t control themselves like normal students and thus need special attention.
But it undeniably lets them know, deep down inside, that they don’t measure up, that they’re not as “good” as everyone else. It becomes who they are, a self-fulfilling prophecy.
It’s human nature. The novelty will where off and motivation will weaken. External rewards alone only work short term and do little to improve behavior over time.
Transferring any responsibility for the behavior in your classroom to someone else—whether it be a parent, principal, or counselor—weakens your ability to do it yourself.

A behavior contract is nothing more than a replacement for a classroom management plan that isn’t being followed. The difference is that a classroom management plan doesn’t label students or chip away at their self-confidence.
